stories.headline: J&K statehood may be restored in near future, says Ramdas Athawale
stories.title: J&K statehood may be restored in near future, says Ramdas Athawale
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 11: Union Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Ramdas Athawale on Sunday said the restoration of statehood to Jammu and Kashmir could take place in the near future, while stressing that the final decision on timing rested with Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah. Addressing a press conference in Srinagar, Athawale, who heads the Republican Party of India (Athawale) and is part of the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance, said the Centre had earlier committed in Parliament to restoring statehood at an appropriate time. He added that he was not in a position to announce any specific timeline. “After the abrogation of Article 370, Union Home Minister Amit Shah ji had given this assurance that statehood to Jammu and Kashmir will be restored. And it can definitely be decided after a few days,” Athawale said. He noted that Modi and Shah were fully aware of the commitment and that the government would consider the issue. The remarks come weeks after the Jammu and Kashmir Assembly, on September 28, passed a resolution seeking the immediate and urgent restoration of full statehood. The resolution, moved by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, was adopted amid a walkout by BJP legislators. It followed the 2024 Assembly elections held after the Supreme Court’s December 2023 directive that elections be conducted and statehood restored “at the earliest.” Athawale said political differences should not affect the allocation of funds or the implementation of development projects. He highlighted the Centre’s ongoing infrastructure push, including improvements in road networks, national highways, tunnels and railway connectivity. He also said the government was working to generate employment for youth by attracting private investment, with several investors expected to invest thousands of crores of rupees in the Union Territory. Referring to the abrogation of Article 370 in August 2019, Athawale said the decision had brought Jammu and Kashmir fully under the Indian Constitution and extended various constitutional provisions and benefits to the region. He maintained that the overall security situation had improved considerably, with a significant reduction in violence, though challenges remained. On the Pahalgam terror attack of April 22, 2025, in which 26 people, mostly tourists, were killed at Baisaran, Athawale said the Centre had taken necessary steps and urged Pakistan to stop supporting terrorism. “Jammu and Kashmir is an integral part of India, and Pakistan should focus on improving its own economy rather than interfering in India’s internal affairs,” he said. He added that people in Pakistan also wanted peaceful relations with India, but political interests were preventing normalisation, and that India did not seek conflict. Athawale said the Centre was ready to extend assistance to the Union Territory and urged the local administration to formulate concrete proposals to address developmental needs. He said he had sought time from Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to discuss issues concerning Jammu and Kashmir and planned to meet Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha to convey the region’s requirements. Recalling his earlier visits to several districts, the minister said he continued to interact with people to understand their concerns and reiterated that development initiatives must benefit people at the grassroots level.

stories.headline: Climate Change Action Plan
stories.title: Climate Change Action Plan
stories.summary: As Jammu and Kashmir is facing extreme impact of climate change, it was heartening to see top brass of government brainstorm to revise Jammu & Kashmir State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC 2.0). Leading from the front, Chief Secretary, Atal Dulloo, chaired a meeting to assess the revised Jammu & Kashmir State Action Plan on Climate Change and called for further refinement of the plan by incorporating clearly defined, department-wise actions, outcomes and timelines up to 2030. Being prepared by the Department of Forest, Ecology & Environment, Jammu & Kashmir State Action Plan on Climate Change envisages providing a comprehensive framework for strengthening climate resilience in J&K while aligning the Union Territory’s climate response with the country’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), the Paris Agreement and the emerging climate risks specific to the region. The Action Plan on Climate Change assumes significance as J&K ranks third among the Himalayan areas which are vulnerable to climate change and fall in the highest seismic zones. J&K is a multi-hazard prone Himalayan region which is vulnerable to natural disasters especially earthquake, floods, landslides, windstorms and soil erosion besides Glacial Lake Flood Outbursts. The climate projections based on IPCC pathways, including SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 state that under the moderate-emission scenario, temperatures are projected to rise by around 1.5°C during 2021–2050. And there will be implications for water resources, agriculture, health and ecosystems. The annual precipitation is projected to increase by around 5 per cent under the moderate-emission scenario and up to 15 per cent under the high-emission scenario. Projections point towards shorter cold seasons and greater variability and intensity of rainfall events in J&K. The climate vulnerability assessment has evaluated 42 indicators across agriculture, water, health and forest sectors, identifying district-specific vulnerabilities and risks to facilitate targeted interventions. The revised climate action plan proposes 55 emission mitigation strategies, with an estimated mitigation potential of 2.6 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent by 2030. These include promotion of solar energy, including floating solar plants, greater utilisation of small hydropower and wind energy, strengthening of grid infrastructure, reduction of transmission and distribution losses, promotion of electric mobility and deployment of Intelligent Traffic Management Systems. Government has proposed 100 adaptation actions across five key sectors along with Disaster Risk Reduction measures including expansion of micro-irrigation, achieving universal household tap-water coverage, rainwater harvesting, strengthening health facilities in underserved areas, restoration of degraded catchment forests with native species. Besides construction of retaining walls and other slope-protection measures at vulnerable locations have also been proposed. The Chief Secretary has rightly emphasised that a climate action plan should translate into clear, actionable and time-bound interventions. Departments have been directed to incorporate actions to be undertaken along with their expected outcomes and milestones, over the period up to 2030. The revised framework should clearly establish who will do what, by when and with what measurable outcome, while ensuring that the interventions are aligned with J&K’s specific ecological, geographical and socio-economic realities. We have observed erratic changes in climatic patterns in J&K for the last several years. Peak winter periods passed snowless with rise in temperatures. Summers too have been warmer and prolonged spells of heat waves. There has been a rise in flash floods triggered by cloudbursts mostly in mountainous regions causing loss of over 30 lives. Kashmir has recorded a 33.4% rainfall deficit and Jammu 21.4% in September. The combined 20-district shortfall of 24.4% falls in the IMD’s deficit category. Under IMD classification, rainfall departures of -19% to +19% are normal, -20% to -59% are deficit and below -60% are large deficits. Departures of +20% to +59% are excess and +60% or more are large excess. Kashmir’s eight districts received 252.8 mm against 379.6 mm normal, a 33.4% deficit. J&K recorded a 24% deficit in June, followed by 35% excess rainfall in July, bringing cumulative June-August precipitation into the normal category despite another shortfall in August. In August, Kashmir recorded a 25% deficit and Jammu 16% below normal. Experts’ blames changing climatic patterns coupled with El Niño for August and September rainfall deficits. Less snowfall in winter coupled with rain deficit in rains in summer has severely affected irrigated agriculture, horticultural productivity, and hydropower generation, thereby posing serious challenges to the region’s water security and climate resilience. It is to be noted that snowmelt accounts for 50 percent of streamflow in Kashmir, making winter snowfall critical for sustaining hydrology and water availability. Reduction of snow cover or snowfall directly translates into diminished spring and summer runoff. Snowfall deficit and higher temperatures in winter poses risk of increased cryosphere-related hazards like permafrost degradation triggered slope failures including debris flows, mudflows, and rock falls and also trigger Glacial Lake Outburst Floods. J&K Government and stakeholders must be serious on implementation of the State Action Plan on Climate Change. Process must be expedited to provide institutional mechanism under SAPCC 2.0, envisaging a Governing Council headed by the Chief Minister to meet annually and an Executive Council chaired by the Chief Secretary to meet twice a year for overseeing implementation and inter-departmental coordination. The revised SAPCC 2.0 must be placed at the earliest before the State Level Steering Committee (SLSC) for formal approval before its submission to the National Level Steering Committee under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) for its early implementation on ground. We must wake again and join efforts to mitigate the effects of climate change. We need to contribute our bit to maintain ecological balance and prevent any activity aimed at endangering nature. Our existence depends on nature and we must co-exist! Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: SC seeks answers from Centre, Police
stories.title: SC seeks answers from Centre, Police
stories.summary: New Delhi, Oct 11: The Supreme Court on Sunday said contempt petitioners, who have alleged violations of the court's direction to ensure no complete prohibition on metro and trains services in Delhi due to a CJP protest, have made out a "prima-facie" case. During a special hearing, a bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued notices to Secretary in the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) Chairperson D Thara. "Having considered the submissions of the counsel for the parties and perused the averments in the contempt petition, we are of the opinion that the petitioners have made out a prima-facie case. "Accordingly, we issue notice upon the alleged contemnors. They are directed to file counter-affidavit to the said petition, including a compliance report, in terms of our order as aforesaid by October 13, 2026. Their personal presence is dispensed with in the meanwhile," the bench said. One of the pleas, filed by advocate Shailendra Mani Tripathi, has contended that the brutal assault on the fundamental rights of citizens and the sheer disregard to the court's orders amount to a deliberate, intentional attempt on the part of the Delhi Metro, the Delhi Police and the Union government, and it must be dealt with an iron hand. The petition has referred to the court's October 9 order that was passed while hearing a separate plea against the closure of 57 metro stations and cancellation of trains to Delhi in view of the protest. The protest call was given by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and some student organisations against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the functioning of the Election Commission (EC). Hearing the petition on Friday, a bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Bagchi and Mohana had directed the Centre to ensure that there was no "complete prohibition" of the movement of metro and trains coming to Delhi on October 10 due to the protest, saying they cannot bring everything to a halt. Though law-enforcement agencies have the right to take steps to restrict unruly movement, citizens should not be unduly harassed, the court had said. The Delhi Metro closed 45 stations from 9 pm on Friday till 6 pm on Saturday for security reasons, according to an advisory. The contempt plea has said notwithstanding the solemn judicial mandate and the assurance recorded before the top court, authorities have "consciously maintained a blanket shutdown across transit corridors, persisted with unwarranted train cancellations, and failed to issue or publicise transparent traffic and transit advisories".

stories.headline: Maharashtra Utility Opts For Thermal+Wind Power For RTC Supply, Cites Rising Data Centre Demand
stories.title: Maharashtra Utility Opts For Thermal+Wind Power For RTC Supply, Cites Rising Data Centre Demand
stories.summary: Nidar Utilities Panvel LLP (NUPLLP), a deemed distribution licensee serving the Panvel Special Economic Zone (SEZ), has secured regulatory approval for the procurement of 5 MW of round-the-clock (RTC) power through a combination of thermal and wind-based generation, citing rising electricity demand from data centres. The Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC), in its latest order adopted tariffs of Rs 5.35/kWh for 2 MW of power from Manikaran Power Limited (MPL) and Rs 4.85/kWh for 3 MW from Arunachal Pradesh Power Corporation Private Limited (APPCPL). The Commission also approved the associated power purchase agreements (PPAs) under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The 2 MW procurement from MPL covers the period from February 1, 2026, to January 31, 2027, while the 3 MW supply from APPCPL is scheduled for April 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027. Both tariffs are applicable at the Maharashtra State Transmission Utility (STU) periphery. Additional Power Requirement According to the petition, NUPLLP's total load is around 18 MW. Its existing power portfolio includes 3 MW of small hydro power, 5 MW contracted with MPL, 7 MW contracted with PTC India, and approximately 3.5 MW procured through power exchanges. The additional short-term procurement is intended to strengthen its contracted supply and meet consumer demand. The growing electricity requirements of data centres are a key factor behind the procurement. NUPLLP stated that its data centre consumers had sought an increase in contract demand from 20,000 kVA to 28,000 kVA. The additional requirement is expected to materialise in phases, prompting the licensee to arrange power accordingly to avoid being left with stranded capacity. Data centres account for approximately 95% of the consumer mix, according to the petition. For the second procurement requirement, NUPLLP initially invited bids for 5 MW of RTC power for the period from April 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027. Following a request from a prospective bidder, it reduced the minimum bid quantity from 5 MW to 2 MW to encourage participation. APPCPL was ultimately selected for 3 MW of supply, with Apraava Renewable Energy Private Limited identified as the generation source. The first procurement involved 2 MW from MPL, with Birla Carbon India Private Limited's Patalganga unit in Maharashtra identified as the source. MERC's order identifies the source for the APPCPL procurement as Apraava Renewable Energy Private Limited, with wind generation specified in the Commission's tariff-comparison discussion. Both procurement requirements received only one bid each. The bidders did not lower their initial price offers during the electronic reverse auction conducted on January 2, 2026. NUPLLP subsequently sought regulatory approval for the discovered tariffs and the PPAs executed with the two suppliers. Reasonable Tariffs: MERC MERC found the tariffs reasonable and comparable with prevailing short-term power prices. The Commission noted that tariffs discovered for short-term RTC power on the DEEP portal ranged from Rs 4.62/kWh to Rs 10/kWh. It concluded that the rates of Rs 5.35/kWh and Rs 4.85/kWh met the requirements for tariff adoption under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003. The petition also highlighted the additional costs associated with procuring power through exchanges. NUPLLP stated that inter-state transmission charges and losses could add approximately Rs 0.65–0.80/kWh when electricity is delivered from the Central Transmission Utility (CTU) regional periphery to Maharashtra's STU periphery. It also pointed to the risk of power not being cleared in certain time blocks during periods of high demand, potentially exposing the licensee to deviation settlement mechanism (DSM) penalties. MERC has also clarified that NUPLLP may procure additional power if demand exceeds its contracted capacity. The licensee can undertake fresh short-term competitive bidding or procure electricity through power exchanges, subject to the applicable Multi-Year Tariff (MYT) Regulations and other legal requirements. The order reinforces the importance of securing dependable power supplies as data-centre electricity demand rises, while allowing NUPLLP to add capacity in phases in line with its consumers' requirements.

stories.headline: A Test of India’s Democratic Conscience
stories.title: A Test of India’s Democratic Conscience
stories.summary: An ordinary Indian does not need to believe that the country is either perfectly democratic or already lost. A more honest position is this: India still has elections, constitutional rights, courts, political parties, a lively society and the capacity for peaceful political change, but the fairness of that system depends on whether institutions remain strong enough to restrain whoever holds power. The central question is therefore not only who wins elections. It is whether citizens can still change governments, criticise leaders, organise collectively, receive reliable information and expect the law to treat them equally. Modern democracies rarely disappear overnight through tanks in the streets. More often, an elected government gradually weakens the institutions that could defeat or restrain it, the media, courts, election systems, civil society, opposition parties and public education. The first warning sign is often political language. When a leader presents himself or his party as the only authentic voice of “the real nation,” and describes opponents as traitors, enemies, vermin or illegitimate citizens, ordinary disagreement is transformed into a struggle between patriots and enemies. This makes compromise appear immoral and allows the ruling side to justify changing the rules in its own favour. The second warning sign is the spread of political nihilism, the belief that nothing can improve, every politician is corrupt, every institution is fake and voting is pointless. Such propaganda does not always ask people to support a particular policy. Sometimes its purpose is simply to make citizens withdraw from public life. A person who believes that participation is useless is less likely to vote, organise, question authority or defend someone else’s rights. India’s Present Tension India’s political environment contains both democratic strength and serious institutional strain. Elections remain competitive, and governments can face defeat; however, organisations such as V-Dem and Freedom House have raised concerns about civil liberties, media freedom, institutional independence and the space available to dissent. V-Dem’s 2025 report classified India as an “electoral autocracy,” while Freedom House’s 2025 assessment rated India “Partly Free”; these are external assessments, not universally accepted judgments, but they identify concerns that should not be dismissed merely because elections continue. The practical meaning is important. A country may hold elections and still become less fair if money, media access, investigative agencies, public institutions and political information are distributed unequally. The question is not whether India has democracy in a formal sense, but whether an ordinary citizen has a meaningful chance to use democratic rights against concentrated power.At the same time, criticism should not become fatalism. India’s voters have repeatedly surprised powerful parties, regional movements remain influential, courts and journalists continue to contest official claims, and citizens still organise around employment, prices, education, land, identity and local rights. Democratic decline is a danger, not an irreversible destiny. The RSS and its allied organisations must be understood as a long-term social and cultural project, not merely as an electoral machine. The BJP is the principal electoral arm, but the broader Sangh Parivar has worked through schools, student groups, labour organisations, service networks, cultural bodies and local institutions. Vidya Bharati, established formally in 1977 and linked to earlier Saraswati Shishu Mandir initiatives, says it operates more than 12,000 schools and serves over 3.5 million students; these figures are associated with the organisation and should be read as institutional claims rather than independent government statistics. This strategy matters because elections change governments, while education and social institutions shape habits, identity and ideas about the nation over decades. The RSS’s centenary is therefore not simply a celebration of organisational longevity; it is also evidence of the power of patient institution-building. There is nothing inherently undemocratic about building schools, social-service organisations or cultural institutions. The democratic question is what they teach, whom they include, whether they encourage critical thought, and whether public institutions remain open to competing visions of India. A plural democracy must allow Hindu cultural organisations to exist, but it must also protect Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Dalits, Adivasis, regional communities, atheists and all others from being treated as lesser citizens. Jammu and Kashmir gives this national question an especially sharp form, because political authority, identity, security and constitutional status are deeply intertwined. The Supreme Court upheld the Union government’s 2019 changes concerning Article 370 in December 2023, directed that Assembly elections be held by September 2024, and stated that statehood should be restored “at the earliest”; later proceedings continued to focus on the unresolved question of restoration. The 2024 Assembly election demonstrated that political participation in Jammu and Kashmir has not disappeared. The National Conference won 42 of the 90 seats, the BJP won 29, Congress won 6, the PDP won 3, and smaller parties and independents won the remaining seats. The regional pattern was also significant: the National Conference-led alliance dominated the Valley, while the BJP was strongest in Jammu. But elections alone cannot settle the question of democratic confidence. Many people in Jammu and Kashmir want not only representatives but also dignity, security, economic opportunity, accountable administration and a clear restoration of political powers. For residents, the difference between a full state government and a Union Territory administration is not abstract constitutional theory, it concerns who controls decisions affecting land, employment, policing, development and everyday life. A fair democratic settlement must also reject two simplifications. Jammu and Kashmir cannot be reduced either to a security problem or to a single political narrative. Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh have different histories, aspirations and political experiences; within each region, minorities, women, young people, displaced communities, border residents and economically vulnerable groups have different concerns. Yet Jammu and Kashmir must confront an uncomfortable reality. Much of its political discourse remains trapped in the past while India is undergoing profound political, economic and technological change. Across both government and opposition, there is a visible shortage of fresh political thinking. Electoral calculations and familiar slogans often substitute for a coherent vision of the future. The future of Jammu and Kashmir will not be secured by elections alone. It requires a new generation of political thinkers, civic leaders, educators and entrepreneurs capable of imagining a future beyond grievance and dependency. Democracies thrive when they create space for new ideas, new leadership and new possibilities. The real question is not whether Jammu and Kashmir has a future. It is whether we possess the vision, courage and intellectual honesty to shape it. Dr. Farooq Wasil is a published author, and an educationist.

article_sentences: Rajya Sabha MP John Brittas and All India Students’ Association president Neha were among several protestors allegedly injured by security forces as they were being detained in the capital on Sunday (October 11, 2026), the second day of a protest called by youth organisations demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Despite the Supreme Court’s directives on Saturday (October 10), around a dozen journalists were detained on Sunday (October 11) while covering the protest at different locations.
There was no official announcement by Delhi.
Police on the total number of detentions on Sunday.

Leader of the Opposition (LoP) and Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, meanwhile, announced a march to the Supreme Court on Monday (October 12), calling the “youth, all opposition parties, civil society groups, all those who believe in democracy and stand by the Constitution of India,” to join the procession.

The unprecedented security arrangements in the New Delhi area — imposed on October 10, and considerably relaxed after the top court’s hearing earlier in the day — are likely to be back on Monday (October 12) in the wake of Mr. Gandhi’s call.
While mobile Internet was restored on Sunday (October 11), residents continued a cautious approach.
Despite the festive season, footfall and business remained low in Connaught Place and the central Delhi area that was still interspersed with police barricades.
Activists of different organisations alleged that they were beaten by security forces, which the Delhi.
Police denied.
The police claimed that the protestors were being adamant and not cooperating at the time of detention.

Meanwhile, Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) leaders who were released on Sunday (October 11) after being detained a day earlier, asserted that the protests would continue till the CEC resigns.

article_sentences: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) had earlier warned of severe weather conditions across Delhi, Haryana, and Punjab, forecasting high-speed winds reaching up to 60 kilometers per hour alongside potential hailstorms.
The overnight tempest also disrupted Navratri celebrations leaving festival organisers scrambling to secure venues.
Visuals from areas like Jantar Mantar and Kalkaji showed waterlogged streets and deserted protest sites as the downpour battered the city.
With waterlogged streets and continuous downpours disrupting early morning routines, authorities urge commuters and residents to stay alert.

Citizens are strongly advised to avoid sheltering under trees or weak structures, steer clear of waterlogged and flood-prone corridors, check real-time traffic updates, and strictly follow official advisories.
According to the weekly weather bulletin issued by the IMD, severe weather warnings and rainfall activity extend across multiple administrative subdivisions and dates.

Northwest Region: Isolated heavy rainfall, thunderstorms, lightning, and hailstorms were forecasted for Haryana, Chandigarh & Delhi, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu-Kashmir-Ladakh-Gilgit-Baltistan-Muzaffarabad, and Uttarakhand on October 11.

Extended Outlook: Scattered-to-fairly widespread rainfall is projected to continue across Northwest India, with specific weather systems affecting Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh & Delhi, and Uttar Pradesh spanning from October 11 through October 16.
Southern and Eastern Systems: Isolated heavy rainfall is expected over Kerala & Mahe and Tamil Nadu, Puducherry & Karaikal during October 16-17.
Additionally, a low-pressure area is likely to form over the Southeast Bay of Bengal around October 13 under the influence of an upper-air cyclonic circulation.

The southwest monsoon withdrawal line continues to pass through Supaul, Ranchi, Sundargarh, Bargarh, Bijapur, Hyderabad, Belagavi and Panjim as of October 11 with conditions becoming favorable for further withdrawal from parts of eastern India, the Northern Peninsula, and northeast India over the subsequent two days.

stories.headline: HC quashes PSA detention over two-year delay in execution
stories.title: HC quashes PSA detention over two-year delay in execution
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 11: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has quashed a preventive detention order issued against Kaiser Hameed Beigh under the Public Safety Act (PSA), holding that the order was based on vague and irrelevant grounds and that an unexplained delay of more than two years in its execution had snapped the required “live and proximate link” between past alleged activities and the need for detention. Justice Rajesh Sekhri passed the judgment while allowing a petition challenging the detention order dated June 25, 2022, issued by the District Magistrate, Anantnag. The High Court had stayed the order on September 11, 2024, before its execution. According to the detention dossier, the Senior Superintendent of Police, Anantnag, had alleged that Beigh was an overground worker of the banned Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) outfit and had allegedly provided shelter and transportation to active terroristss. The authorities also cited his previous detention under the PSA in 2021 and apprehensions ahead of the Shri Amarnath Yatra as reasons for seeking fresh preventive detention. However, the petitioner argued that the allegations were vague, no fresh activities had been attributed to him after the earlier incidents, and the detention order was passed despite the absence of any immediate threat justifying his detention. He also challenged the delay in executing the order, pointing out that he had remained available and continued attending court proceedings. The authorities opposed the petition, maintaining that the detention order had been passed after considering the police dossier and that the petitioner’s alleged activities posed a threat to the security of the State. After examining the record, Justice Sekhri observed that the detention order appeared to have been passed on the apprehension that the petitioner’s alleged links with the banned outfit made it risky to keep him at liberty during the Amarnath Yatra. The court noted that the petitioner was regularly attending proceedings before the Additional Sessions Judge, Anantnag, in the single FIR of 2019 cited against him. Relying on the Supreme Court’s judgment in Additional Secretary to Government of India v. Alka Subash Gadia, the High Court held that pre-execution challenges to detention orders can be entertained in limited circumstances, including where orders are based on vague or irrelevant grounds or are issued for an improper purpose. The court further observed that preventive detention must be supported by a strong and immediate connection between past conduct and the present necessity for detention. The unexplained delay of over two years, it held, had severed that connection. “Viewed from any angle, the impugned order does not sustain in the eyes of law,” the court observed, quashing the detention order and allowing the petition.
